source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2023) Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models (FunSearch, Nature)
finding: Gap 3. FunSearch found a size-512 cap set in n=8, 'larger than previously known'. It also raised the cap set capacity lower bound from 2.2180 to 2.2202. Only 4 of 140 experiments found the 512 set.
numbers: n=8 cap set 512 found in 4/140 runs (about 3%). Capacity lower bound 2.2180 -> 2.2202 via partial admissible set A(24,17) of size 237,984. Full I(12,7) set: bound 2.2184, found in 60% of runs. I(15,10) implies C >= 2.219486. Known upper bound C <= 2.756.
limits: The prior n=8 record of 496 is NOT stated on the fetched page (read through a summariser); treat 496 as unverified. The paper says the n=8 result was particularly challenging to reproduce.
agent_relevance: A verified-scorer loop does find new results, but the n=8 hit was rare (3% of runs). Selection by exact score beats any judge; report hit rate over repeated runs, not the best run.

source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2023) FunSearch, online bin packing and compute
finding: FunSearch evolved a bin-packing heuristic that beat first fit and best fit on every test set. The heuristic was trained on OR1-size instances and generalised to larger ones.
numbers: Excess bins over L2 bound, first fit / best fit / FunSearch: OR1 6.42/5.81/5.30%; OR2 6.45/6.06/4.19%; OR3 5.74/5.37/3.11%; OR4 5.23/4.94/2.47%; Weibull 5k 4.23/3.98/0.68%; 10k 4.20/3.90/0.32%; 100k 4.00/3.79/0.03%. Compute: samples on the order of 10^6; 15 samplers and 150 CPU evaluators; Codey (PaLM 2 family) without fine-tuning; islands reseeded every 4 hours (worst half dropped); prompt uses k=2 programs.
limits: Main text gives no numbers for the no-LLM or StarCoder ablations (supplement not opened), so the equal-compute question stays open. Works only with an efficient evaluator and rich score signal; the authors say proof generation is out of scope.
agent_relevance: About 1 million model samples for a result. Cost is the price of verified search; a cheap exact scorer is the precondition. Relevant to G7 but not a control against best-of-N.

source: Sahu, Larochelle, Charlin, Pal (2025) ReviewerToo: Should AI join the program committee?
finding: Gap 9. On 1,963 ICLR 2025 submissions (balanced accept/reject), the best LLM reviewer set-up (meta-reviewer over all personas, gpt-oss-120b) got 81.8% binary accuracy against 83.9% for the average human reviewer. This is far better than the n=10 Beel test suggests.
numbers: Binary accuracy: Meta(all) 81.8%; Average of personas 75.1%; Default single reviewer 70.6%; Meta with top-3 74.8%; human average 83.9% (n=540 reviews); top 1% human 92.4%. 5-way accuracy: Meta(all) 52.5%, human avg 37.6%, top-1% human 56.4%. Supervised baselines: BERT fine-tuned 63.7%, XGBoost 55.8%.
quote: 81.8% accuracy for the task of categorizing a paper as accept/reject compared to 83.9% for the average human reviewer
limits: Judged against final accept/reject, which is itself noisy. Permissive persona over-predicts accept, critical persona over-predicts reject. Human-LLM Cohen kappa only 0.1-0.2. Weak on methodological novelty and theory. Table columns were read from misaligned text extraction.
agent_relevance: A single reviewer prompt is near 70%; ensembles reach about 80%. A model judge can be a screen but one persona is biased. Use an ensemble of opposed personas only as a filter, never as final selector.

source: Sahu et al. (2025) ReviewerToo, bias and sycophancy findings
finding: LLM reviewers get more positive after reading author rebuttals: F1 drops after rebuttal because false positives rise. Persona agreement varies from moderate to negative.
numbers: Cohen kappa about 0.5 for Majority and Default; near zero or negative for Permissive and Critical personas; human-LLM kappa 0.1-0.2. Metareviewer aggregation raised agreement with ground truth.
limits: Authors say the rebuttal effect may hint at sycophancy; not tested directly.
agent_relevance: An agent that reads its own critic's response to a rebuttal may drift to accept. Keep the critic blind to the author's defence (supports G8 independence).

source: Schmidgall and Moor (2025) AgentRxiv: collaborative autonomous research
finding: Gap 8. A single agent lab (o3-mini, N=40 paper generations) that could read its own earlier papers raised gpt-4o-mini MATH-500 accuracy from 70.2% to 78.2% (+11.4% relative). That gain is single-agent memory, not multi-agent.
numbers: Single lab: 70.2 -> 78.2% (method SDA). Transfer of SDA: +3.3% on average over other benchmarks and models; MedQA 79.6 -> 85.6 (+7.5%). Three parallel labs with shared repository: 79.8% at one setting; best 13.7% relative. Mean time per paper 1.36 h (max 11.9 h).
limits: The best technique is selected by accuracy on the same MATH-500 test set (text: new highest accuracy on the test set), so selection-on-test inflates the 78.2%; the transfer to other sets (+3.3%) is the cleaner number. Agents also hallucinate results and reward-hack (section 4.1). No no-memory control at equal token cost found in the text read.
agent_relevance: Memory of earlier results helps a single agent, but the headline number is contaminated by test-set selection. Keep a held-out set that the loop never sees (G7).

source: Schmidgall and Moor (2025) AgentRxiv, hallucination and duplicate effort
finding: Agent Laboratory hallucinates experiment results (seemingly realistic numbers) and parallel labs duplicate effort.
numbers: Parallel labs reached 78.2% while exploring similar techniques ('redundancy' noted). Per-paper runtime 0.09 h to 11.9 h.
limits: Self-reported limitation section; no counts of hallucinated papers extracted in my read.
agent_relevance: Any shared memory must store code-run outputs, not prose claims, or hallucinated results become prior knowledge.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap, appendix D correlations
finding: Gap 2. Pre-execution reviewer scores barely predict post-execution scores. For AI ideas the excitement correlation is negative.
numbers: AI ideas, ideation vs execution: Pearson novelty -0.019, excitement -0.321, effectiveness 0.172, overall -0.092 (Spearman: excitement -0.386, effectiveness 0.110, overall -0.092). Human ideas: Pearson novelty -0.084, excitement 0.205, effectiveness 0.022, overall 0.158 (Spearman overall 0.124). N=43 executed ideas in total.
limits: Small N (about 20 per arm); NLP prompting ideas only; wide intervals. Still no condition shows a strong positive link. Spearman row for AI novelty (0.077) is misaligned in extraction.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 2 for NLP: idea-stage LLM-judged score is not a usable proxy for result quality. Rank by executed outcome.

source: Si et al. (2025) Ideation-execution gap, overall score vs breakdown
finding: After execution, the overall score correlates strongly with effectiveness: reviewers weight whether it worked.
numbers: Overall vs effectiveness r = 0.654 (Table 11); change in overall score correlates highly with change in novelty and excitement (Table 12).
limits: Reviewer ratings of execution, not independent ground truth.
agent_relevance: Outcome (does it work) dominates the final judgement, so a code-run check is the right primary signal.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: time profile of o1 vs human
finding: Gap 5. On a small subset, o1 beats the human baseline in the first hours but plateaus after about 1 hour; humans overtake after 24 hours.
numbers: 3-paper subset: human ML PhDs best-of-3 41.4% after 48 h vs o1 26.6%. Agents run up to 12 h by default; a 36 h extended o1 run graded at 1, 3, 6, 12, 36 h. Best agent on full PaperBench 21.0%. Code-Dev variant: o1 43.4%. 3 repeats, SEM bars.
quote: o1's scores mostly plateau after the first hour
limits: Tiny human sample (3 to 4 papers), one model; plateau may reflect scaffold (agent stops early) rather than the model. Authors say the agent fails to strategize beyond the first hour.
agent_relevance: Compute helps early, then flat without a mechanism for planning over long horizons. A schema needs state and re-planning, not just more samples.

source: La Cava et al. (2021) SRBench, ground-truth recovery vs noise
finding: Gap 10. AI Feynman solves exact Feynman equations at 53% with no noise, nearly twice the next method (GP-GOMEA, 27%). Above noise 0.01 four other methods (DSR, gplearn, AFP_FE, AFP) recover exact solutions more often.
numbers: Noise levels 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1; 10 random seeds per problem. On Strogatz ODE problems AI Feynman is not significantly different from others. Best black-box method is Operon, which struggles to recover exact formulas despite near-perfect test scores.
quote: AIFeynman may be brittle in application to real-world and/or noisy data
limits: About AI Feynman, not LLM-based SR. SRBench has no LLM method, so whether LLM-SR is noise-fragile is NOT answered here.
agent_relevance: Closes the first half of gap 10: structure-exploiting search is noise-brittle. Second half (LLM-SR on noisy real data) stays open.

source: Nova (2024) iterative planning and search for novel idea generation
finding: Gap 1 (partial). Iterating plan, retrieve, generate gives more unique ideas than baselines at the same NUMBER of ideas (100 per method), but token cost is not matched or reported in the text read.
numbers: Each method generated 100 ideas; duplicate threshold cosine 0.8; Nova over 80% unique; 3.4x more unique novel ideas than baseline; 619 ideas scored 4 and 2521 scored 5 in Swiss pairwise scoring; 37.5% of the human top-4 ideas; 17.53% of worst-4. Ablation: without planning unique ideas stay flat (42.4 at step 2, 44.1 at step 3).
limits: Matched idea count is not matched compute (planning plus retrieval calls cost extra). Judge is an LLM pairwise ranker; novelty judged by LLM plus embedding.
agent_relevance: Search with retrieval widens diversity, but gap 1 stays open because there is no equal-token comparison.

source: Multi-workflow novelty study (2026) Evaluating novelty in AI-generated research plans
finding: Gap 1 (partial). Five ideation architectures compared on 30 expert-proposal evaluations; decomposition and long-context pipelines had highest novelty, reflection-only the lowest.
numbers: Mean novelty 3.57, feasibility 2.80, impact 3.47 (0-5; 6 experts x 5 proposals = 30 ratings). Best novelty 4.17/5, reflection-based 2.33/5. Correlations: novelty-feasibility r=0.23; feasibility-impact 0.44 or 0.56 (table text misaligned).
limits: Only 30 ratings; no token matching; no plain-sampling arm. Not a test of generate-test-select vs best-of-N.
agent_relevance: Architecture differences exist but cannot be separated from compute differences. Gap 1 remains open.

source: IEEE Spectrum report on AI co-scientist at Imperial College (bacterial gene transfer)
finding: Gap 6 (partial). In one external test, co-scientist's top hypothesis matched an unpublished mechanism (viral tails borrowed from neighbouring species). Some hypotheses were wrong; a runner-up has only early results.
numbers: No error rate or hypothesis counts given ('a handful of solutions'). n = 1 question.
limits: Journalistic account built on the lab that benefited; no independent audit, no denominator.
agent_relevance: One anecdote is not a rate. Do not cite as replication.

source: King et al. (2024) Genesis: towards the automation of systems biology research
finding: Gap 7. The Robot Scientist group's own review gives few numbers. Adam found functions of locally orphan yeast enzymes; Eve's AI selection beat standard screening by econometric modelling; an automatically built yeast diauxic-shift model added 92 genes (+45%) and 1,048 interactions (+147%).
numbers: Genesis target: 1,000 bioreactors, 1,000 hypothesis-led cycles per day, aim of 100-fold cost-benefit (aim, not result). LGEM+ proposed 2,094 candidate model-improvement hypotheses.
limits: Written by the system's own developers; no hit rates for Adam here. Genesis is incomplete (12 of 48 bioreactor units).
agent_relevance: Classical robot scientists are not quantitatively comparable to LLM agents on shared benchmarks; none report hits per hypothesis in this document.

source: Williams et al. (2015) Cheaper faster drug development validated by repositioning drugs against neglected tropical diseases (Eve)
finding: Gap 7. Eve's active-learning screen used 4,800 compounds for training and picked from the other 9,600 in three loops of 96. TNP-470 selectively inhibits P. vivax DHFR.
numbers: About 14,400 compounds (Maybridge HitFinder) plus about 1,600 approved drugs; throughput over 10,000 compounds/day; assay engineering about 1 person-month, about $15k; TNP-470 IC50 0.16 uM vs over 165 uM for human DHFR (about 1000-fold). Econometric model: cost-optimal to screen one third to one half of the small library.
limits: The page read (via summariser) gave no hit-rate-versus-random figure or confirmed-hit count; developer-authored.
agent_relevance: Active selection saves screening cost only when each experiment is cheap; same logic as a code-run scorer.

source: Scientific American / secondary reports on Robot Scientist Adam
finding: Search snippet only: Adam tested 20 hypotheses on genes for 13 enzymes, 12 confirmed (secondary report); King called the results modest but real.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers without checking King et al. 2009 Science.
agent_relevance: If correct, 60% hit rate on tests drawn from a tight, well-modelled space; not comparable to open-ended LLM hypotheses.
